newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico reaps results in safflower promotion push.
newsitem.headline: Mexico reaps results in safflower promotion push.

text.p: Mexico is promoting more plantings of safflower, an unfashionable but high-yield oilseed that Mexico previously produced in abundance.

"Safflower is a good alterntive (to other oilseeds) at the moment," said Jorge Puga, who heads up a grains trading trust focussing again on safflower here in the capital of the western state of Jalisco.
Jalisco is home to Mexico's most numerous and powerful oilseed crushers and the safflower promotional campaign here is beginning to reap results.
In the last two crop cycles, the surface area under safflower production has tripled in Jalisco. In this upcoming cycle 1996-1997, plantings are expected to soar again.

"It is possible that the surface area reaches between 9,000 and 10,000 hectares (this 1996-1997 cycle)," said Amador Ramirez Rodriguez, director of agriculture for the state's Rural Development Ministry.

Back in 1994-1995, only 1,584 hectares were planted in Jalisco, rising to 5,200 hectares in 1995-1996. Consequently, State output is seen rising to 28,000 tonnes this cycle from the paultry 4,000 tonne output recorded two cycles ago.

That should make Jalisco start to rival Mexico's traditional safflower states, notably Sonora in the north and should be a fundmental factor in the expected increased national output in the calendar year 1996.

Production is seen rising to 150,000 tonnes from 80,000 tonnes in 1995, by still a far cry from the 480,000 tonnes produced in 1980. Throughout the 1980s and early 1990s output gradually dipped, reaching a trough of 47,000 tonnes in 1992.
According to data from the Edible Oils Chamber of Jalisco, national crushers milled a little over 80,000 tonnes of safflower in 1995, all from the national production that year.
Crushing yielded 50,091 tonnes of meal and 30,214 tonnes of oils, the chamber said in a report.
Dwindling safflower production had forced Mexico to start importing large quantities of oilseeds, such as soybeans, to meet the national demands for vegetable oils and margarines.
"Because there is shortage of this product for the crushers, a promotion was started back in 1995... and we have had good results," Rodriguez explained.
The promotional campaign also aimed to improve seed varieties and also pinpoint best land conditions for safflower. Both also have yielded positive results, Rodriguez said.
Crushers and growers have even signed mutal support accords to boost yields. Another has crushers promising to buy up all safflower planted, Rodriguez said.
That too is paying off. Oil contents have risen to a range of between 42 to 44.5 percent in earmarked areas against a national average of 35 percent oil content, he added.

Another part of the promotion is focused on making sure growers have all market information, tendancies and price and weather information at their fingertips before they plant. Trust manager Puga said they send out two information bulletins per day to make sure growers are up to date.
Safflower farmers, many clad in traditional leather sandals, are often seen out of the fields, with pocket calculators in their hands making sure their crop is on track.
Farmer Mario Andrade, from the south of Jalisco state, recently switched to safflower from wheat. "I am (financially) better off planting safflower than other grains," he said.
"It is hard work learning to calculate the crop, because before we just planted and waited to see what happened, but I do not want to leave my children without land," he added.
